title: Additional Notes
section: Daily unique users are not the same as period unique users
text:
Daily unique users are not the same as period unique users
Summing daily unique users gives a measure of user-days, not distinct people over the full period.
For distinct people over a longer period, use a cumulative unique user field such as mtd_unique_users or ytd_unique_users.

title: Additional Notes
section: Metrics can be reported over different timespans
text:
Metrics can be reported over different timespans
Most metrics are meaningful over more than one window. The three standard reporting windows are month-to-date, year-to-date, and since the April 22, 2026 public launch. How you select a window depends on the kind of metric.
Additive metrics (sign-ins, MFA attempts, success rates, averages) are computed by aggregating daily rows, so the window is just the date bounds in the WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '<start>' AND DATE '<end>' clause. The same query covers any window; only the start date changes:

Month-to-date: first of the current month (for example, 2026-06-01)
Year-to-date: 2026-01-01
Since launch: 2026-04-22

Set the end date to the reporting date.
Cumulative unique-user metrics cannot be derived by filtering a date range, because summing daily unique_users counts user-days, not distinct people. Instead, pick the pre-computed column that matches the window and take its latest value:

Month-to-date: mtd_unique_users
Year-to-date: ytd_unique_users

Never sum these cumulative columns across rows.
There is no cumulative since-launch column. The since_apr22_unique_users field that previously provided it has been removed: the cumulative count is computed by the IBM Verify API, which sees only the most recent 366.5 days of source data, so a since-launch total silently truncates once launch is more than a year in the past. The mtd_ and ytd_ windows are unaffected because they fall inside that horizon.
This limit does not affect the additive metrics above. Those are aggregated from the daily rows we store on our side, which are retained beyond a year, so a date-bounded since-launch window over an additive metric stays correct however far back it reaches. See the data retention note in the catalog.

title: Additional Notes
section: Weighted averages should be used for call centre averages
text:
Weighted averages should be used for call centre averages
When calculating average call length or average delay across multiple weeks, use a weighted average based on calls_answered.
A simple average of weekly averages may give too much influence to low-volume weeks.

title: Additional Notes
section: Internal applications should usually be excluded from external adoption reporting
text:
Internal applications should usually be excluded from external adoption reporting
Which applications count as internal is recorded in rp.service.is_internal, not in this document. Resolve it through rp.alias, which maps the application names IBM Verify and Google Analytics use back to a single service:
SELECT al.alias
FROM   rp.alias al
JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
WHERE  s.is_internal
Query the list rather than pasting it into a filter. A service is reclassified by editing the source spreadsheet, and a query holding its own copy of the list will not notice. The same subquery works as a NOT IN in SQL and as an anti_join() in dbplyr; both forms appear in SSO Events by Application.
Whether to exclude internal applications at all depends on the reporting question.

title: Google Analytics
text:
Metrics derived from the CanadaLogin GA4 property, in the google_analytics schema. See the Data Catalog for the underlying tables.
Task success rates are computed from GA4 funnels: named, ordered sequences of page or event steps, defined as version-controlled YAML rather than a private GA4 UI exploration. A funnel’s exact steps can change as CanadaLogin’s own pages change, so metrics on this page describe the general calculation and point to that YAML on GitHub as the definitive, current source, rather than hard-coding step names that may already be out of date by the time they’re read.

Task Success Rate
The proportion of users who started a given task in CanadaLogin and reached that task’s defined finishing point, measured from Google Analytics 4 funnel data.
This is a family of metrics, not a single number: each funnel declares its own task success rate as a step_ratio in its YAML definition on GitHub - one funnel step counted as the entry, another counted as the exit, both measured as GA4 activeUsers over the same reporting window. The entry and exit steps for each funnel are described below as of this writing, but the YAML is the canonical, versioned source - see funnel_src/funnels/ in the canadalogin-reporting-data-pipeline repo. Check the YAML before trusting a step name quoted here.
Alternative names:

funnel completion rate
task completion rate
funnel success rate


Sign in
Funnel definition: sign_in.yaml.
Entry is the first taggable step of the sign-in flow (the “enter your email” screen); exit is reaching MFA selection, the last step Google Analytics can see. This is not a full sign-in completion rate. A successful sign-in redirects off-site to IBM Verify and back to the relying party with no page in between, so GA4 has no event to mark true completion - reaching MFA is the closest proxy available. See the funnels catalog entry for the RESERVED_TOTAL and window_incomplete conventions this table shares with funnel_metrics.


Sign up
Funnel definition: sign_up.yaml.
Entry is the first step of the sign-up flow, after accepting Terms and Conditions; exit is the account-creation confirmation screen. Unlike sign-in, this is a true completion signal - the confirmation page is a real, first-party GA4 event.
Calculation. Each funnel’s task success rate is already computed and stored as one row per window in funnel_metrics: the exit step’s activeUsers divided by the entry step’s, for that funnel run. There is no ratio to compute by hand - filter to the funnel and metric, and read value. Query funnel_metrics_current rather than funnel_metrics directly, so a future funnel version bump can’t silently blend two definitions together. Filter breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL' for the overall rate across all relying parties; substitute a specific relying party name for a per-RP figure.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Sign in:
SELECT
    window_end,
    value AS task_success_rate
FROM google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
WHERE funnel_id = 'sign_in'
  AND metric_id = 'task_success'
  AND window_days = '7'
  AND breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL'
  AND NOT window_incomplete
  -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND CAST(window_end AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-14' AND DATE '2026-08-03'
ORDER BY window_end;
Sign up:
SELECT
    window_end,
    value AS task_success_rate
FROM google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
WHERE funnel_id = 'sign_up'
  AND metric_id = 'task_success'
  AND window_days = '7'
  AND breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL'
  AND NOT window_incomplete
  -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND CAST(window_end AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-14' AND DATE '2026-08-03'
ORDER BY window_end;


Sign in:
tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "funnel_metrics_current")) |>
  filter(
    funnel_id == "sign_in",
    metric_id == "task_success",
    window_days == "7",
    breakdown_value == "RESERVED_TOTAL",
    !window_incomplete,
    # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    as.Date(window_end) >= as.Date("2026-07-14"),
    as.Date(window_end) <= as.Date("2026-08-03")
  ) |>
  select(window_end, task_success_rate = value) |>
  arrange(window_end)
Sign up:
tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "funnel_metrics_current")) |>
  filter(
    funnel_id == "sign_up",
    metric_id == "task_success",
    window_days == "7",
    breakdown_value == "RESERVED_TOTAL",
    !window_incomplete,
    # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    as.Date(window_end) >= as.Date("2026-07-14"),
    as.Date(window_end) <= as.Date("2026-08-03")
  ) |>
  select(window_end, task_success_rate = value) |>
  arrange(window_end)






Interpretation notes. The queries above use window_days = '7', a rolling weekly rate recomputed nightly on a 7-day window ending each date. Three window lengths exist, and switching between them is a one-line change:

'1' is the same metric on a single day. It is the noisiest of the three, but it is the only one that shows the exact date something changed.
'7' is the usual default. Every window holds one of each weekday, so day-of-week effects wash out.
'28' is a rolling four-week window. It is the steadiest of the three and the one to use for monthly reporting, but a step change takes 28 days to show up in it fully, so it is a poor way to check whether a fix worked.

All three are partition-key strings, not numbers, in this schema. Windows within one window_days overlap, so consecutive rows are not independent readings: one unusual day moves 7 weekly rows and 28 monthly ones. A value of NULL means nobody reached the entry step that window (an undefined rate, not a true zero) - such rows are rare but real, and an average that treats them as 0.0 will read too pessimistic.
These two funnels are not directly comparable to each other: sign-in’s rate stops at MFA for the structural reason described above, so it reads lower than a true completion rate would, while sign-up’s rate is a real completion figure. Comparing the two numbers as if they measured the same kind of finish line will overstate the sign-in/sign-up gap.

title: Platform
text: Platform metrics for CanadaLogin, in the sre schema. Currently, both tables are derived from the CanadaLogin Platform team’s CanadaLogin_MTTR_Dashboard Google Sheet (maintained by hand in the CDS Google Drive) and fetched by the sre-mttr-sheets-fetcher Lambda using Google Sheets API 6am ET every Monday. They share one source and grain (one row per incident); they differ only in history: mttr_current holds the latest state of each incident, while mttr_history accumulates a dated snapshot of every incident on each upload.

title: Platform
text:
mttr_current
The latest known state of every CanadaLogin incident, one row per incident.
Each row is a single incident. The table is overwritten on each upload with the most recent values, so it never grows beyond the current incident set. For point-in-time history, see mttr_history.
Keywords: MTTR, MTTA, MTTM, incident, incident response, postmortem, severity, reliability, SRE, mean time to resolve

Provenance
Fetched automatically every Monday at 06:00 ET from the CanadaLogin MTTR Dashboard Google Sheet using the sre-mttr-sheets-fetcher Lambda. Each upload overwrites this table wholesale with the current incident state and appends a dated snapshot to mttr_history.

Updated: Weekly, Every Monday 06:00 ET
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Yinlin Zhang (Data and Research team) or Obie Okongwu (CL Platform Team)

mttr_history
The append-only companion to mttr_current: same source, columns, and provenance, but instead of holding only the latest state it accumulates a dated snapshot of every incident on each upload.
Each row is one incident (incident_id) as it appeared on one snapshot date, so an incident’s metrics can change from one snapshot to the next as it is re-triaged. A row is unique on (incident_id, date).

uptime_timeseries
One row per upptime bot commit per site. The upptime bot commits to the cds-snc/status-statut history YAML files once per day (~23:2x UTC) as a daily snapshot, plus additional commits immediately when a status change is detected mid-day.

Provenance
Fully automated. No manual upload required. Sourced from the GitHub Commits API for each site’s history file (history/<slug>.yml).

Updated: Daily, at ~04:00 ET
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Yinlin Zhang (Data and Research team)

varchar
Hive partition key: the UTC date of the commit (YYYY-MM-DD). Use in WHERE date = '...' or WHERE CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN ... filters.

varchar
UTC timestamp of the upptime bot’s commit (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS). On a normal day this is the daily snapshot at ~23:2x UTC. On an outage day earlier commits record when the site went down or recovered.

varchar
Upptime site identifier, same six values as in sre.uptime_summary.

Short label, same six values as in sre.uptime_summary.

varchar
Ping result at the moment of this commit: up, down, or unknown.

bigint
HTTP status code at the moment of this commit. 200 on a normal day; 0 or 503 when down. null if unparseable.

Response time in milliseconds at the moment of this commit. Single-ping measurement at commit time, not a daily average. null if unparseable.





Notes
response_ms is a single-ping measurement. It records the response time at the exact moment of the upptime bot’s commit, not a daily average. For averaged response times use sre.uptime_summary (response_day_ms, response_week_ms, etc.), which are computed from all 288 five-minute pings.
status = 'down' rows count detection events, not outage duration. Each down row is one commit, one moment when upptime detected a failure. For total minutes of downtime on a given date, use the daily_minutes_down JSON column in sre.uptime_summary.

title: Google Analytics
text:
property_traffic
Property-wide daily traffic for the CanadaLogin GA4 property, with no dimension beyond the day.
Each row represents one day of aggregate site-wide traffic.
Keywords: Google Analytics, GA4, traffic, sessions, active users, page views

Provenance
Pulled daily from the GA4 Data API (runReport) for the CanadaLogin property, via a Lambda authenticating through Google Cloud Workload Identity Federation (no stored service account key). Written as JSONL, then cast to typed Parquet by a Glue ETL job.

Updated: Daily, at 07:00 ET
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Colin Douglas
Location: s3://<transformed-bucket>/google_analytics/property_traffic/



Fields
One row per date.








Field Name
Type
Description




date
string
The reporting day, as a partition key (for example, “2026-07-23”)


sessions
bigint
Number of sessions started on this day, site-wide


activeusers
bigint
Number of distinct active users on this day, site-wide


newusers
bigint
Number of users on this day who had not been seen before


screenpageviews
bigint
Number of page views on this day, site-wide





Notes
activeusers is de-duplicated by GA4 within the day; it is not the sum of per-page unique users. This table is the collection canary for the GA4 pipeline: because it carries no dimension beyond date, a property-wide active-user collapse here distinguishes “GA stopped collecting” from “one page or one funnel’s tag broke,” which page_traffic rows alone cannot do.
screenpageviews here should equal SUM(screenpageviews) from page_traffic for the same date - the two tables’ only currently-summable metric, and a useful integrity check between them. sessions and activeusers do not reconcile the same way across the two tables (GA4 de-duplicates each within its own dimension combination), so do not expect them to match.

title: Google Analytics
text:
funnels
Step-by-step counts for each defined GA4 funnel (currently sign_in and sign_up), for a given reporting window.
Each row represents one step of one funnel run, for one relying party (or the funnel’s total across all relying parties).
Keywords: Google Analytics, GA4, funnel, funnel step, task success, drop-off, abandonment, relying party

Provenance
A funnel is defined as YAML, not SQL: one file per funnel in funnel_src/funnels/ in the canadalogin-reporting-data-pipeline repo. A dedicated Lambda turns each funnel’s YAML into a GA4 Data API runFunnelReport request (via Workload Identity Federation, same auth pattern as property_traffic) and writes the result as JSONL. The YAML on GitHub is the canonical definition of what each funnel measures - which pages or events count as which step, in what order, and over what population. This page describes the table shape; it does not enumerate step names, because they are versioned in that YAML and can change between funnel versions.

Updated: Daily, at 06:30 ET (a nightly sweep; see Notes)
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Colin Douglas
Location: s3://<transformed-bucket>/google_analytics/funnels/



Fields
One row per funnel_id per funnel_version per window_days per window_end per funnelstepname per breakdown_value.








Field Name
Type
Description




funnel_id
string
Partition key. Which funnel this row belongs to (for example, “sign_in”, “sign_up”) - matches a filename under funnel_src/funnels/ on GitHub


funnel_version
string
Partition key. The funnel definition’s version at the time this row was run. A plain integer, but typed string by the crawler - see Notes


window_days
string
Partition key. Length of the reporting window this row summarizes: “1” for a nightly monitoring run, “7” for a rolling weekly rate, “28” for a rolling four-week rate


window_end
string
Partition key. Last date (inclusive) of the reporting window, as text (for example, “2026-07-23”)


funnelstepnumber
bigint
The step’s 1-indexed position in the funnel


funnelstepname
string
The step’s name, as declared in the funnel’s YAML on GitHub. Not a closed set - see Provenance


breakdown_dimension
string
The bare GA4 dimension a funnel’s breakdown: block splits by (currently always “rp_name”, the relying party)


breakdown_value
string
The relying party this row covers, or the sentinel RESERVED_TOTAL for the funnel’s grand total across all relying parties (including any past GA4’s 15-value breakdown cap) - see Notes


activeusers
bigint
Distinct active users who reached this step, for this relying party, within the window


funnelstepcompletionrate
double
GA4’s own step-over-step completion rate (this step’s users over the previous step’s)


funnelstepabandonments
bigint
Users who reached this step but did not reach the next one


funnelstepabandonmentrate
double
funnelstepabandonments as a proportion of this step’s activeusers


window_start
string
First date (inclusive) of the reporting window, as text. Derivable from window_end and window_days, but stored for convenience


window_incomplete
boolean
true if this window was trimmed to the funnel’s valid_from/valid_to bounds (see Notes) - exclude these rows from any trend read as a full window





Notes
A funnel’s step names, order and population can change between versions - always check GitHub, not a memory of a prior version. Every CanadaLogin funnel has already had at least one step renamed or re-scoped since it was first defined (see the task success rate metric for a worked example). funnel_version exists so old and new definitions coexist rather than silently overwriting each other: always pin funnel_version in a query, or use the funnels_current view, which resolves the newest version per date automatically. Summing or averaging across versions blends two different definitions of the funnel into one meaningless number.
RESERVED_TOTAL is a real GA4 sentinel, not a relying party. A funnel breakdown caps at 15 distinct values; RESERVED_TOTAL is GA4’s grand total across all relying parties, including any beyond that cap, and is the correct number to read as the funnel’s overall rate.
window_incomplete rows are written, not dropped, and must be excluded from a trend. A window that reaches earlier than a funnel’s valid_from (or later than valid_to) is trimmed and flagged rather than skipped, so a scheduled job keeps running as a tagging boundary recedes.
activeusers is de-duplicated within its own window and is not additive across windows. Summing seven daily (window_days = "1") rows for a week, for example, is not the same query as one window_days = "7" row for that week - repeat users within the week are counted once by the 7-day row and once per day they appeared by the daily rows. Never sum activeusers across rows with different window_end or window_days values.

title: Google Analytics
text:
funnels_current
A view over funnels that resolves the current funnel_version automatically. Query this instead of funnels directly unless a specific past version is genuinely what’s wanted.
Each row is the same as a funnels row, restricted to the newest funnel_version available for that row’s (funnel_id, window_days, window_end).
Keywords: Google Analytics, GA4, funnel, funnel version, current version

Definition
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW funnels_current AS
WITH latest_per_date AS (
  SELECT funnel_id, window_days, window_end,
         MAX(CAST(funnel_version AS integer)) AS current_version
  FROM funnels
  GROUP BY funnel_id, window_days, window_end
)
SELECT f.*
FROM funnels f
JOIN latest_per_date d
  ON  f.funnel_id   = d.funnel_id
  AND f.window_days = d.window_days
  AND f.window_end  = d.window_end
  AND CAST(f.funnel_version AS integer) = d.current_version;


Provenance

Updated: Live view, not scheduled
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Colin Douglas



Fields
Same as funnels. SELECT f.* passes every base column through unchanged; the view’s own current_version column (used only to resolve the join) is not exposed.


Notes
The partition keys are still typed string in the view’s output, the same as the base table - MAX(funnel_version) on the view still sorts lexically wrong if you ignore that the view has already picked one version per row. Query it the same way you’d query funnels: filter with quoted string literals (WHERE window_days = '7', not = 7), and don’t re-aggregate across funnel_version since the view has already resolved it.
Resolution is per (funnel_id, window_days, window_end), not a global max per funnel. If a funnel bumps from version 1 to version 2 partway through its history, dates before the bump still resolve to version 1 (version 2 was never run for them) and dates from the bump onward resolve to version 2 - one continuous time series, not a series that vanishes before the bump. This only holds because versions of the same funnel are assumed to measure the same underlying thing; it would not be a safe pattern for two versions that represent genuinely different metrics.

This table deliberately does not carry the raw step values a ratio was computed from - only the result. The inputs are recoverable by joining back to funnels on the same (funnel_id, funnel_version, window_days, window_end, breakdown_value), if they’re needed.

A metric is recomputed automatically when its funnel’s funnel_version bumps (the same nightly job backfills every past window under the new version), but adding a metrics: block to a funnel for the first time also triggers a one-time backfill across that funnel’s entire already-landed history - so a metric’s earliest window_end is not necessarily the date the metric was defined.

title: IBM Verify
text:
app_login_counts
Daily SSO event counts for each CanadaLogin-integrated application.
Each row represents one application on one day, summarizing that application’s usage and unique-user reach for the day. This table records what IBM Verify calls the sso event type, filed under application usage and raised when someone who is already signed in reaches an application.

A since_apr22_unique_users field (cumulative distinct users since the April 22, 2026 public launch) was previously provided here. It has been removed from the pipeline because the source API retains only the most recent 366.5 days of data, so a since-launch cumulative count cannot be maintained once launch is more than a year in the past. See the retention note on the IBM Verify catalog overview.
Unlike auth_total_logins, these counts are not inflated by second factors. The per-authentication-method event inflation described there only happens when a person signs in to CanadaLogin itself. Reaching an integrated application uses the session they already hold: CanadaLogin issues the application a freshly minted assertion or token, the person enters no password or second factor, and one handoff records one SSO event. total_logins and successful_logins still count events rather than people, because one person can reach an application repeatedly. text:

Daily, CanadaLogin-wide authentication event totals across all applications.
Each row represents one day and summarizes overall CanadaLogin authentication activity. This table records what IBM Verify calls the authentication event type, raised each time someone presents an authentication method.
app_login_counts records a different event type (sso, which IBM Verify files under application usage). Figures from the two tables are therefore not comparable and must never be added together or presented side by side. There is also no per-application breakdown here.

The reporting day as a text date (for example, “2026-05-21”). Mirrors from_date





Notes
unique_users, failed_logins, and successful_logins are daily values. The mtd_, ytd_, and rolling_365d_ unique-user fields are cumulative and should not be summed across rows; take the latest value within the window instead.
rolling_365d_unique_users is null before 2026-06-13, its implementation date.
A since_apr22_unique_users field (cumulative distinct users since the April 22, 2026 launch) was previously provided here. It has been removed from the pipeline because the source API retains only the most recent 366.5 days of data, so a since-launch cumulative count cannot be maintained once launch is more than a year in the past. See the retention note on the IBM Verify catalog overview.
When a user signs in to CanadaLogin itself, IBM Verify records each authentication method as a separate event. Entering a username and password followed by a second factor like an OTP counts as two successful events. A mistyped password that is then entered correctly, followed by a correct OTP, counts as three events: two successful and one failed. Both successful_logins and failed_logins are therefore inflated relative to the number of distinct sign-in sessions.
This inflation applies only to signing in to CanadaLogin itself. Reaching an integrated application does not add to these counts at all: it raises an SSO event on app_login_counts instead. CanadaLogin uses the session the person already holds and issues the application a freshly minted assertion or token, so the person enters no password and no second factor.
Summing successful_logins is therefore a misleading indicator of actual user engagement. Instead, use the unique_users field, which is daily active users, and is a measure of the number of users who engaged with the system in a given day.

title: IBM Verify
text:
mfa_activity
Daily multi-factor authentication (MFA) activity, broken down by factor type and outcome.
Each row represents the count of MFA attempts for a single combination of day, MFA factor type, and result.
Keywords: MFA, multi-factor, second factor, OTP, FIDO2, authentication, security

Provenance
Queried directly from the IBM Verify production instance via API.

Updated: Daily, at 6am America/Toronto
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Yinlin Zhang



Fields
One row per day per mfa_type per result.








Field Name
Type
Description

timestamp
Start of the reporting day (midnight)


to_date
timestamp
End of the reporting day (23:59:59)


mfa_type
string
The MFA factor used. One of “sms_otp”, “fido2”, “kq”, “totp”, “voice_otp”, “qr”, “ibm_verify_push”, “email_otp”


result
string
Outcome of the MFA event. One of “success”, “failure”, or “sent”


count
integer
Number of MFA attempts for this day, factor, and result


fetched_at
timestamp
When the aggregation last fetched this row

string
The reporting day as a text date (for example, “2026-05-31”). Mirrors from_date





Notes
Only OTP factor types (sms_otp, email_otp, voice_otp) generate a “sent” event, because they are issued before the user responds. Successfully clearing one of these challenges therefore counts as two events: first a “sent” event, then either a “success” or “failure” event depending on how the user responds. It is possible to generate multiple “success”/“failure” events on a single “sent” event if the user inputs their OTP incorrectly first and then correctly. Non-OTP factor types (fido2, kq, totp, ibm_verify_push) have no “sent” event and produce only “success”/“failure” rows.
When calculating MFA usage metrics, de-duplicate accordingly: count “sent” events for OTP factors (sending an email OTP but not using it is still usage), and “success”/“failure” events for non-OTP factors. Summing “sent” alone would silently drop every non-OTP factor.
When calculating success rate metrics, use the number of successful events divided by the sum of the success and failure events, excluding “sent”.

title: Jira (PSOM)
text:
Tables in the jira schema, populated by the weekly PSOM Jira Service Management sync pipeline.
Each Monday at ~6:00 AM ET, the psom-weekly-sync Lambda fetches a full snapshot of all tickets from the PSOM project (jtickets.atlassian.net) and writes it as a Parquet partition in S3. The Glue crawler then updates the Athena table schema.

title: Jira (PSOM)
text:
PSOM
Weekly snapshot of all PSOM Jira Service Management tickets.
One row per Jira issue per weekly snapshot. Each Monday run writes a full snapshot of all current PSOM tickets to a new date= partition. Previous partitions are preserved as an audit trail, enabling point-in-time analysis.
Jira source: jtickets.atlassian.net, project PSOM, fetched via POST /rest/api/3/search/jql with full comment history via /rest/api/3/issue/{key}/comment.
Keywords: jira, psom, tickets, service requests, SLA, support

Provenance
Queried from PSOM Jira Cloud via API by the psom-weekly-sync Lambda function.

Updated: Weekly, every Monday at ~06:00 ET
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Yinlin Zhang (Data and Research team)



Fields
One row per Jira issue per weekly snapshot (date partition).








Field Name
Type
Description




date
varchar
Partition key: the date the Lambda ran (YYYY-MM-DD).


key
varchar
Jira ticket key, e.g. PSOM-42.


summary
varchar
One-line ticket title.


description
varchar
Full ticket description, extracted from Atlassian Document Format (ADF) to plain text.


issue_type
varchar
Jira issue type name, e.g. Email Request, Partner Support Request form.


status
varchar
Current workflow status, e.g. Done, Canceled, Escalated to PTT, Escalated to Auth PT, Ready to archive.


status_changed
varchar
ISO 8601 timestamp when the ticket’s status category last changed.


priority
varchar
Priority level, e.g. High, Normal, Low, Critical.


assignee
varchar
Display name of the current assignee; empty string if unassigned.


reporter
varchar
Display name of the person who reported the ticket.


creator
varchar
Display name of the person who created the ticket (may differ from reporter).


created
varchar
ISO 8601 timestamp when the ticket was created.


updated
varchar
ISO 8601 timestamp of the most recent field or comment update.


due_date
varchar
Due date in YYYY-MM-DD format; empty string if not set.


labels
varchar
Semicolon-separated list of labels applied to the ticket; empty string if none.


request_type
varchar
JSM service request type name, e.g. New Access Request. Empty for tickets created internally through Jira rather than the customer-facing portal (all PSOM tickets so far), which never set a request type.


request_participants
varchar
Semicolon-separated display names of request participants (CC’d users).


organizations
varchar
Semicolon-separated names of JSM organizations the request is associated with.


sla_first_response_due
varchar
ISO 8601 datetime the “Time to first response” SLA must be (or was) met by, per the SLA goal. For an open ticket this is the upcoming breach deadline; for a closed cycle, when the cycle stopped. Empty if no SLA clock.


sla_first_response_breached
varchar
"True" if the first-response SLA was missed (no agent response within the agreed 4-hour window), "False" if it was met or is still within the window, "" if no SLA clock. Stored as a string, not a native boolean.


sla_time_to_done_due
varchar
ISO 8601 datetime the “Time to done” SLA must be (or was) met by, per the SLA goal. For an open ticket this is the upcoming breach deadline; for a closed cycle, when the cycle stopped. Empty if no SLA clock.


sla_time_to_done_breached
varchar
"True" if the resolution SLA was missed (ticket not resolved within the agreed 16-hour window), "False" if it was met or is still within the window, "" if no SLA clock. Stored as a string, not a native boolean.


comment_count
bigint
Total number of comments on the ticket.


comments
varchar
JSON array string of all comments. Each element: {"author": "...", "created": "...", "updated": "...", "body": "...", "internal": false}. The body is ADF-extracted plain text. The internal flag is true for JSM internal notes.


fetched_at
varchar
UTC timestamp when the Lambda wrote this row (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS).





Notes
All timestamp columns (created, updated, status_changed, sla_*_due, fetched_at) are stored as varchar.
SLA fields (sla_first_response_*, sla_time_to_done_*) are populated for tickets with an active JSM SLA clock. The *_breached columns hold the strings "True"/"False", not a native boolean, so compare against 'True'/'False' (not a bare boolean) and cast if you need one. "False" covers both SLAs that were met and open tickets still inside their window, so a breach rate computed on a single snapshot is a lower bound: an open ticket counted as "False" today can still breach later. Snapshots up to and including date=2026-07-06 predate the SLA pipeline fix and have these columns empty; from date=2026-07-07 on they are populated. Exclude empty-string rows when calculating breach rates.
Each weekly run adds a new date= partition. All previous partitions are retained, so you can compare snapshots across weeks to track status changes over time.

title: Relying Parties
text:
Reference tables for identifying and grouping the services that use CanadaLogin, in the rp schema. They hold no measurements. They exist to give the analytics tables a shared service identifier, so that IBM Verify sign-in counts and Google Analytics funnel steps can be reported against the same list of services.
service holds one row per relying party, with its names, operator, and launch date. alias maps each of the many strings the source systems use for a service back to that service’s rp_id.
Both tables come from one hand-maintained Google Sheet, read every weekday by the rp-sync Lambda in cds-snc/canadalogin-reporting-data-pipeline. That pipeline owns the table structure. Do not change it from this side.

title: Relying Parties
text:
service
One row per relying party: a service that uses CanadaLogin to sign its users in. Services that run more than one application in CanadaLogin appear once here, not once per application.
Keywords: Relying party, RP, service, application, department, operator, GC org

Provenance
The list is maintained by hand in the CanadaLogin Relying Parties Google Sheet. The rp-sync Lambda reads the sheet every weekday and writes a single Parquet file to S3, then triggers a Glue crawler to refresh the table in Athena. The table is not partitioned and the file is overwritten in place, so this table holds current state only and keeps no history.

Updated: Weekdays, at 06:00 ET
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Colin Douglas
Location: s3://canadalogin-reporting-transformed/rp/service/



Fields








Field Name
Type
Description




rp_id
bigint
Identifier for the relying party. Assigned by hand in the source sheet and stable across refreshes. Joins to rp.alias.rp_id.


service_name_en
varchar
English name of the service. Free text.


service_name_fr
varchar
French name of the service. Free text.


operator
varchar
The organization that runs the service, typed by hand. Display only, see the note below.


gc_orgid
bigint
The gc_orgID of the operating organization, or 0 for entities that are not in the originating dataset.


is_internal
boolean
Is the service internal facing, rather than something the public signs in to?


launch_date
varchar
Approximate date the service launched to the public, as YYYY-MM-DD. Stored as text.


fetched_at
timestamp(3)
When the Lambda last read the source sheet, in UTC.





Notes
Group by gc_orgid, not operator. gc_orgid comes from the GC Organization Names and Codes dataset. IDs can be resolved to bilingual names through that dataset or the companion tool, cds-snc/gcorg-resolver.
gc_orgid = 0 means not applicable. The organization running the service has no entry in the GC organization dataset, so there is no ID to record. For these rows, group on the operator value instead.
launch_date is a string, so cast both sides when comparing. Comparing it against an R value that looks like an ISO date fails with TYPE_MISMATCH: Cannot apply operator: varchar = date, because RAthena casts ISO-format strings to a SQL DATE literal.
This is not a complete inventory of relying parties. A service is added to the sheet when it shows up in IBM Verify or the analytics data, so a service that is live but has no traffic yet will be missing. Do not use count(*) here as the denominator for “how many services use CanadaLogin”.

title: Relying Parties
text:
alias
One row per name that refers to a relying party. The same service is called different things in different systems, and this table maps each of those strings back to a single rp_id.
Use it to join tables that have no shared service identifier, such as ibm_verify.app_login_counts.application_name and the rp_name breakdown in the Google Analytics funnel tables.
Keywords: Relying party, RP, alias, application name, crosswalk, lookup, join

Provenance
Maintained by hand in the same CanadaLogin Relying Parties Google Sheet as rp.service, read every weekday by the same Lambda and written as a single Parquet file. Not partitioned, overwritten in place, current state only.

Updated: Weekdays, at 06:00 ET
Steward: EDCP Data and Research Team
Contact: Colin Douglas
Location: s3://canadalogin-reporting-transformed/rp/alias/



Fields








Field Name
Type
Description




alias
varchar
The string that refers to the service, exactly as the source system writes it.


rp_id
bigint
The relying party this alias refers to. Joins to rp.service.rp_id.


source
varchar
Where the alias was first encountered, one of IBM Verify or Google Analytics. Record keeping only, see the note below.


fetched_at
timestamp(3)
When the Lambda last read the source sheet, in UTC.





Notes
Join on alias alone. Do not filter on source. source records where the name was first seen, not which system the name belongs to. Filtering by it before joining will silently drop matches for any alias that turns up in both systems.
One service, several aliases. A service has as many rows here as it has names. For example, MyCGC is MyCGC in Google Analytics but both MyCGC - CGC - .NET - Prod and MyCGC - CGC - Power Pages - Prod in IBM Verify. Joining a fact table through this lookup is a many-to-one join, so aggregate after the join, not before.
Not every string in the analytics tables is an alias. The rp_name breakdown in the Google Analytics funnel tables also contains RESERVED_TOTAL (the all-services rollup), (not set), and the empty string. None of these are services, and an inner join drops them. If you are reconciling totals, exclude RESERVED_TOTAL explicitly rather than relying on the join to remove it.
Aliases are exact strings, not patterns. They are matched literally, with no trimming or case folding. A new application name in IBM Verify will not resolve until it is added to the source sheet by hand.

title: Call Centre
text:
Metrics in this section are calculated from call centre activity and topic data.
Call centre metrics are useful for understanding support demand, service responsiveness, caller wait times, average call duration, and common reasons for contact. The source data is weekly, so these metrics are typically reported at a weekly level or aggregated across weeks.
The relevant call centre tables are:
date_range_start and date_range_end are stored as text, so date-range filters cast them to DATE before comparing to date literals.

title: Call Centre
text:
Activity Metrics
Metrics in this section describe call centre operations, sourced from call_centre.weekly_activity_report.

Calls Accepted
The number of calls accepted by the call centre during a reporting period.
This metric is useful for tracking call centre demand and understanding how contact volume changes over time.
Alternative names:

calls received
accepted calls
weekly call volume
call centre demand
number of calls handled by the queue

Calculation. Use calls_accepted by reporting period, or sum across periods for a total.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(calls_accepted AS BIGINT) AS calls_accepted
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;
Total over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_accepted AS BIGINT)) AS total_calls_accepted
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    calls_accepted
  )
Total over a period:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_calls_accepted = sum(calls_accepted, na.rm = TRUE)
  )






Interpretation notes. Calls accepted may not be identical to calls answered, depending on call centre definitions and routing logic.


Calls Answered
The number of calls answered by call centre agents during a reporting period.
This metric is also used as a weighting variable when calculating weighted average call length and weighted average delay.
Alternative names:

answered calls
calls handled
agent-answered calls
completed calls
calls taken by agents

Calculation. Use calls_answered by reporting period, or sum across periods for a total.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT) AS calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;
Total over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT)) AS total_calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    calls_answered
  )
Total over a period:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_calls_answered = sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )






Interpretation notes. Calls answered is commonly used as the weighting field when combining weekly average call length or delay values.


Average Call Length
The average length of answered calls.
The overall average call length is calculated as a weighted mean of avg_call_length_seconds, weighted by calls_answered. This is preferable to a simple average of weekly averages because weeks with more answered calls should contribute more to the overall result.
Alternative names:

average call duration
average handle time
average length of call
typical call length
average time on call

Calculation. Calculate a weighted average of weekly average call length, weighted by the number of answered calls.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Weighted average over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(avg_call_length_seconds AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS weighted_avg_call_length_seconds
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';
By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(avg_call_length_seconds AS DOUBLE) AS avg_call_length_seconds,
    CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT) AS calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;


Weighted average over a period:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_avg_call_length_seconds =
      sum(avg_call_length_seconds * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    avg_call_length_seconds,
    calls_answered
  )






Interpretation notes. Use a weighted average rather than a simple average of weekly averages. A simple average may give too much influence to low-volume weeks.


Average Delay
The average delay before calls are answered.
This metric is useful for understanding caller wait times and call centre responsiveness. Like average call length, it should be calculated as a weighted mean to avoid low-volume weeks distorting the result.
Alternative names:

average wait time
average delay before answer
caller wait time
time to answer
average queue delay

Calculation. Calculate a weighted average of weekly average delay, weighted by the number of answered calls.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Weighted average over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(avg_delay_seconds AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS weighted_avg_delay_seconds
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';
By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(avg_delay_seconds AS DOUBLE) AS avg_delay_seconds,
    CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT) AS calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;


Weighted average over a period:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_avg_delay_seconds =
      sum(avg_delay_seconds * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    avg_delay_seconds,
    calls_answered
  )






Interpretation notes. Average delay should be interpreted alongside call volume. A low-volume week can produce unusual wait times that should not dominate the overall result.


Abandonment Rate
The proportion of accepted calls that were abandoned before being answered.
This metric is useful for understanding how often callers give up while waiting. It is closely tied to wait times: rising delay often drives rising abandonment.
Alternative names:

abandon rate
call abandonment rate
drop rate
proportion of calls abandoned

Calculation. Divide the sum of calls_abandoned by the sum of calls_accepted over the selected reporting period. Summing the raw counts gives a volume-weighted rate; do not average the weekly calls_abandoned_pct column.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_abandoned AS DOUBLE))
        / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_accepted AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS abandonment_rate
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    abandonment_rate =
      sum(calls_abandoned, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_accepted, na.rm = TRUE)
  )






Interpretation notes. The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Read it together with average delay; a spike in abandonment usually coincides with longer waits.


Answer Rate
The proportion of accepted calls that were answered by an agent.
This metric is the complement of abandonment and any other non-answered outcomes. It summarizes how much of incoming demand the call centre actually served.
Alternative names:

answer ratio
proportion of calls answered
pickup rate
calls answered rate

Calculation. Divide the sum of calls_answered by the sum of calls_accepted over the selected reporting period.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE))
        / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_accepted AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS answer_rate
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    answer_rate =
      sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_accepted, na.rm = TRUE)
  )






Interpretation notes. The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. A high answer rate with rising delay can still indicate strain: calls are answered eventually, but callers wait longer to reach an agent.


Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
The proportion of calls answered within 60 seconds.
This metric is a standard call centre service-level measure of how quickly the queue is cleared. The source data stores only the weekly proportion (pct_answered_within_60s), not the underlying within-60s count, so combine weeks with a weighted average rather than re-deriving from counts.
Alternative names:

service level
SLA
grade of service
percent answered within 60 seconds
speed of answer

Calculation. Calculate a weighted average of pct_answered_within_60s, weighted by calls_answered.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(pct_answered_within_60s AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS service_level_60s
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    service_level_60s =
      sum(pct_answered_within_60s * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )






Interpretation notes. The result is a proportion between 0 and 1. Because only the weekly proportion is stored, the weighted average is an approximation of the true within-60s rate, but it is far closer than a simple average of weekly values.


Average Handle Time
The average total time agents spend per call, including any after-call wrap-up.
avg_handle_time_seconds covers more than avg_call_length_seconds: it adds wrap-up work after the caller disconnects. Like the other averages, combine weeks with a weighted mean.
Alternative names:

AHT
average handling time
total handle time per call
average talk plus wrap time

Calculation. Calculate a weighted average of avg_handle_time_seconds, weighted by calls_answered.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(avg_handle_time_seconds AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS weighted_avg_handle_time_seconds
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_avg_handle_time_seconds =
      sum(avg_handle_time_seconds * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )






Interpretation notes. Average handle time is always at least as large as average call length. A widening gap between the two points to growing after-call work.


Calls per Active User
Call centre volume divided by the size of the active user base, so you can compare support demand across weeks even as the user base grows.
Raw call volume moves partly because the number of people using CanadaLogin changes. Normalizing by active users takes that out and leaves how often a typical user needed to phone in on a given day. The figure is scaled to calls per 100 active users to keep it in a readable range.
Alternative names:

call centre contact rate
normalized call volume
support contacts per active user
calls per 100 users
support demand

Calculation. For each call centre reporting week, take calls_accepted from call_centre.weekly_activity_report, subtract that week’s test_calls, and divide by the total user-days in that week, then multiply by 100. User-days is the sum of ibm_verify.auth_total_logins.unique_users over the days whose date falls inside the week’s date_range_start to date_range_end, so the numerator and the denominator cover the same span of days. A weekly call count over weekly user-days is a per-day rate. The two tables store their dates as text, so both sides of the join are cast to DATE.
Use calls_accepted, not calls_answered: accepted counts everything that reached the queue, so an abandoned call still counts as demand. test_calls is a subset of accepted and is large enough at current volumes to be worth subtracting.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    w.date_range_start,
    w.date_range_end,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted AS BIGINT) AS calls_accepted,
    CAST(COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS test_calls,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted - COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS calls_excl_test,
    AVG(a.unique_users) AS avg_daily_active_users,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted - COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS DOUBLE)
        / SUM(a.unique_users) * 100 AS calls_per_100_dau
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report AS w
JOIN ibm_verify.auth_total_logins AS a
    ON CAST(a.date AS DATE)
       BETWEEN CAST(w.date_range_start AS DATE) AND CAST(w.date_range_end AS DATE)
GROUP BY w.date_range_start, w.date_range_end, w.calls_accepted, w.test_calls
ORDER BY w.date_range_start;


weekly <- tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  select(date_range_start, date_range_end, calls_accepted, test_calls)

dau <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  select(dau_date = date, unique_users)

weekly |>
  cross_join(dau) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(dau_date) >= as.Date(date_range_start),
    as.Date(dau_date) <= as.Date(date_range_end)
  ) |>
  group_by(date_range_start, date_range_end, calls_accepted, test_calls) |>
  summarise(
    avg_daily_active_users = mean(unique_users, na.rm = TRUE),
    user_days = sum(unique_users, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    test_calls = coalesce(test_calls, 0),
    calls_excl_test = calls_accepted - test_calls,
    calls_per_100_dau = calls_excl_test / user_days * 100
  ) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    calls_accepted,
    test_calls,
    calls_excl_test,
    avg_daily_active_users,
    calls_per_100_dau
  )






Interpretation notes. Both sides are per-day averages over the same Sunday to Saturday week: average daily calls over average daily active users. On a typical day, roughly this many calls came in per 100 active users. This converts cleanly to a percentage, e.g., 2 calls per 100 users means 2% of users called on a given day.
Watch the units. Dividing a whole week of calls by one day’s active users reads about seven times too high. Normalizing by user-days avoids that and holds up for a partial week, since the day count comes from the data rather than a hardcoded 7. avg_daily_active_users is output for auditing only; the rate comes from the sum.
A call centre week runs Sunday to Saturday, from the report’s own date_range_start and date_range_end. The IBM Verify metrics anchor weeks on Monday, so the two do not line up; the join and the denominator follow the call centre boundaries.
A week appears only once daily active user data exists for it, so the series starts near the April 22, 2026 launch.

title: Call Centre
text:
Topic Metrics
Metrics in this section describe why people contact the call centre, sourced from call_centre.weekly_topic_dump. Because a single call can generate multiple topic rows, these metrics count topic records rather than distinct calls. Clean statobject before grouping, since it often carries leading, trailing, or repeated whitespace.

Call Topic Share
The percentage of all topic records represented by each call topic.
This is useful for understanding the relative importance of each call driver compared to the overall volume.
Alternative names:

share of calls by topic
percentage of calls by reason
topic distribution
call reason mix
contact driver share

Calculation. Count records by cleaned topic, then divide each topic count by the total count across all topics.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH topic_counts AS (
    SELECT
        REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ') AS call_topic,
        COUNT(*) AS topic_count
    FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
    GROUP BY REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ')
)

SELECT
    call_topic,
    topic_count,
    CAST(topic_count AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(topic_count) OVER (), 0) AS topic_share
FROM topic_counts
ORDER BY topic_count DESC;


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  mutate(
    call_topic = str_squish(statobject)
  ) |>
  count(call_topic, name = "topic_count") |>
  mutate(
    topic_share = as.double(topic_count) / sum(topic_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(topic_count))






Interpretation notes. Topic share is useful for comparing relative demand across contact reasons. Interpret alongside total call volume.


Top 10 Call Topics
The ten most common call topics in the call centre topic data.
This is useful for quickly identifying the most common reasons people contact the call centre.
Alternative names:

top 10 call reasons
most common call topics
top contact drivers
main reasons for calling
top caller issues

Calculation. Count records by cleaned topic, calculate topic share, and return the top 10 by topic count.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH topic_counts AS (
    SELECT
        REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ') AS call_topic,
        COUNT(*) AS topic_count
    FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
    GROUP BY REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ')
),

topic_shares AS (
    SELECT
        call_topic,
        topic_count,
        CAST(topic_count AS DOUBLE)
            / NULLIF(SUM(topic_count) OVER (), 0) AS topic_share
    FROM topic_counts
)

SELECT
    call_topic,
    topic_count,
    topic_share
FROM topic_shares
-- sort on topic_count desc, then call_topic asc to break ties deterministically
ORDER BY topic_count DESC, call_topic
LIMIT 10;


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  mutate(
    call_topic = str_squish(statobject)
  ) |>
  count(call_topic, name = "topic_count") |>
  mutate(
    topic_share = as.double(topic_count) / sum(topic_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  # sort on topic_count desc, then call_topic asc to break ties deterministically
  arrange(desc(topic_count), call_topic) |>
  head(10)






Interpretation notes. The top 10 view is useful for quick reporting but may hide important lower-volume issues. In cases where there are not many calls, it may be useful to limit this list to a top 5, or to truncate ties at the end of the list.

title: IBM Verify
text:
Metrics in this section come from IBM Verify, which records two different kinds of event. It raises an authentication event when someone presents an authentication method to CanadaLogin: a password, then a second factor. It raises an SSO event when someone who is already signed in reaches a partner service, and files that one under application usage. These are separate event types, so a figure taken from one is never comparable to a figure taken from the other.
A user signs in to CanadaLogin once and gets a session. Reaching a partner service afterwards does not sign them in again: CanadaLogin uses the session it already holds and issues the partner a freshly minted assertion or token. One sign-in, then as many handoffs as the user needs.
“Sign-in” is prose only. No table counts it, so it is never an output column name or an axis label, and names a metric only where that metric is labelled an estimate.
The relevant IBM Verify tables are:
Internal applications. Internal applications are typically excluded from public-facing adoption metrics. Which ones are internal comes from rp.service.is_internal, resolved to IBM Verify’s application names through rp.alias:
Use the subquery rather than a pasted list, so the classification stays in one place. See the internal applications note in notes.qmd.

title: IBM Verify
text:
CanadaLogin Metrics
Metrics in this section describe CanadaLogin overall, across all applications, sourced mainly from ibm_verify.auth_total_logins (the estimated sessions metric also draws on ibm_verify.mfa_activity).

Authentication Events
The total number of authentication events CanadaLogin recorded, including both successful and failed attempts.
An authentication event is what IBM Verify records when someone presents an authentication method. A single sign-in raises more than one: the password is one event, a second factor is another.
Alternative names:

authentication event volume
total authentication attempts
total sign-in attempts

Calculation. Sum failed_logins and successful_logins over the selected reporting period.
To track volume over time, bin the same sum by week. Truncating from_date to the week groups each day into its Monday-anchored bin, so the result is one authentication event total per Monday-to-Sunday week.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    SUM(failed_logins + successful_logins) AS total_authentication_events
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28';
By week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', from_date) AS week_start,
    SUM(failed_logins + successful_logins) AS total_authentication_events
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', from_date)
ORDER BY week_start;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_authentication_events = sum(failed_logins + successful_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(from_date, "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start) |>
  summarise(
    total_authentication_events = sum(failed_logins + successful_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(week_start)






Interpretation notes. This counts authentication events. It does not count sign-ins, and it does not count people. A single sign-in that uses a second factor records more than one successful event (see the auth_total_logins caveat), so the total runs ahead of how often people actually signed in. No table in the catalog counts sign-ins directly. Use a unique-user metric when the question is about reach. In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so a low count in a boundary week may reflect fewer days rather than a real dip in volume.


Authentication Success Rate
The proportion of authentication attempts that succeeded, across all of CanadaLogin. A failed attempt can be a wrong password or a failed second factor.
This metric is useful for monitoring overall authentication health. A sustained drop can indicate a service problem, a misconfigured application, or elevated attack traffic inflating the failure count.
Alternative names:

sign-in success rate
overall authentication success rate
successful authentication proportion

Calculation. Divide the sum of successful_logins by the sum of all attempts (successful_logins + failed_logins) over the selected reporting period.
To track the metric over time, bin the same calculation by week. Truncating from_date to the week groups each day into its Monday-anchored bin, so the result is one success rate per Monday-to-Sunday week.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS authentication_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28';
By week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', from_date) AS week_start,
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS authentication_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', from_date)
ORDER BY week_start;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    authentication_success_rate =
      sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(successful_logins + failed_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(from_date, "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start) |>
  summarise(
    authentication_success_rate =
      sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(successful_logins + failed_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(week_start)






Interpretation notes. The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Read it alongside authentication event volume: a low success rate on very low volume may just be noise, while the same rate on high volume is a real signal. In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so treat boundary weeks with caution when comparing trends.
This rate is computed over authentication methods, not sessions. When signing in to CanadaLogin, IBM Verify records each method as its own event, so a mistyped password is a failed event even when the user then succeeds and completes the sign-in (see the auth_total_logins caveat). The figure measures how often individual authentication steps succeed, not how often a sign-in ultimately completes. The per-application rate counts a different IBM Verify event type, the handoff to a relying party with no factors entered, so the two rates are not comparable.


Completed Sign-In Sessions (Estimated)
An estimate of the number of completed sign-in sessions to CanadaLogin over a selected reporting period, where a session is one user getting all the way through the sign-in flow regardless of how many authentication methods it took.
Alternative names:

estimated sign-in sessions
estimated login count
sign-in sessions

Calculation. A completed session has exactly one successful first-factor event (the password) plus zero or more successful second factors. Both kinds of success are lumped together in successful_logins on auth_total_logins, while the second-factor successes are counted separately on mfa_activity. Subtracting the second from the first leaves one event per session: the first-factor success. So sum successful_logins over the window and subtract the sum of mfa_activity.count where result = 'success', restricted to the factors that can complete a sign-in.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH first_factor AS (
    SELECT SUM(successful_logins) AS successful_events
    FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
    -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
),

second_factor AS (
    SELECT SUM(count) AS mfa_successes
    FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
    -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
      -- outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
      AND result = 'success'
      -- email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
      -- successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
      AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
)

SELECT
    first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes
        AS estimated_completed_sessions
FROM first_factor
CROSS JOIN second_factor;


sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

successful_events <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(successful_events = sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(successful_events)

mfa_successes <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
    result == "success",
    # email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
    # successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types
  ) |>
  summarise(mfa_successes = sum(as.double(count), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(mfa_successes)

successful_events - mfa_successes






Interpretation notes. The estimate works because each session contributes exactly one first-factor success no matter how many second factors it used:









Session type
successful_logins
Subtracted MFA successes
Net (= sessions)




Password only
1
0
1


Password + SMS OTP
2
1
1


Password + step-up (2 factors)
3
2
1


Mistyped password, then OTP
2 (the failure lands in failed_logins)
1
1


Sign-up email validation
0
0
0



email_otp is excluded because a successful email_otp does not increment successful_logins. It validates an email address at sign-up rather than completing a sign-in.
The estimate rests on two assumptions:

Passwordless and FIDO-first logins are undercounted. A session whose only factor is FIDO2 is one event in successful_logins and also a fido2 success in mfa_activity, so it nets to zero. The figure is therefore a slight underestimate.
The two tables are assumed to count sign-in second-factor successes the same way. Both derive from the same IBM Verify event stream, which makes this plausible, but it is not guaranteed by anything in the data catalog.

Because of these assumptions, label the result as estimated wherever it is reported, and never present it as an exact session count. When the question is about distinct people rather than sessions, prefer unique_users (daily active users), which needs no assumptions: a user cannot be a unique user without completing a sign-in.


Sign-Ins per Active User (Estimated)
How often a typical user signs in to CanadaLogin over a calendar month, counting only the users who signed in at all that month.
This builds on Completed Sign-In Sessions and inherits its estimate and its assumptions. The denominator is mtd_unique_users read on the month’s last day, so the reporting window has to be whole calendar months.
Alternative names:

sign-in frequency
sessions per active user
monthly sign-in rate

Calculation. Per calendar month, estimate sessions as in Completed Sign-In Sessions: sum successful_logins and subtract the successes of the factors that can complete a sign-in (sms_otp, voice_otp, fido2). Divide by mtd_unique_users on the month’s last day, which is that month’s distinct signed-in users.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH first_factor AS (
    SELECT
        date_trunc('month', from_date) AS month,
        SUM(successful_logins) AS successful_events
    FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
    -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
    GROUP BY 1
),

second_factor AS (
    SELECT
        date_trunc('month', from_date) AS month,
        SUM(count) AS mfa_successes
    FROM ibm_verify.mfa_activity
    -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
    WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
      -- outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
      AND result = 'success'
      -- email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
      -- successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
      AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
    GROUP BY 1
),

active_users AS (
    SELECT month, mtd_unique_users AS monthly_active_users
    FROM (
        SELECT
            date_trunc('month', from_date) AS month,
            mtd_unique_users,
            ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', from_date)
                ORDER BY from_date DESC
            ) AS day_rank
        FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
        -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
        WHERE from_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
    )
    -- mtd_unique_users accumulates through the month, so the last day holds
    -- the month's distinct signed-in users
    WHERE day_rank = 1
)

SELECT
    first_factor.month,
    first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes
        AS estimated_sessions,
    active_users.monthly_active_users,
    CAST(
        first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes AS DOUBLE
    ) / NULLIF(active_users.monthly_active_users, 0)
        AS sign_ins_per_active_user
FROM first_factor
JOIN second_factor ON first_factor.month = second_factor.month
JOIN active_users ON first_factor.month = active_users.month
ORDER BY first_factor.month;


sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

first_factor <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-08-31")
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(from_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(successful_events = sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE))

second_factor <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-08-31"),
    # outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
    result == "success",
    # email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
    # successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(from_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(mfa_successes = sum(as.double(count), na.rm = TRUE))

active_users <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    from_date >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    from_date <= as.Date("2026-08-31")
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(from_date, "month")) |>
  # mtd_unique_users accumulates through the month, so the last day holds
  # the month's distinct signed-in users
  filter(from_date == max(from_date, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(month, monthly_active_users = mtd_unique_users)

first_factor |>
  inner_join(second_factor, by = "month") |>
  inner_join(active_users, by = "month") |>
  mutate(
    estimated_sessions = successful_events - mfa_successes,
    sign_ins_per_active_user =
      as.double(estimated_sessions) / as.double(monthly_active_users)
  ) |>
  select(month, estimated_sessions, monthly_active_users, sign_ins_per_active_user) |>
  arrange(month)






Interpretation notes. This is per active user, not per registered user. A user who does not sign in at all that month is not counted in the denominator.
Sessions carry the undercount described in Completed Sign-In Sessions.


Cumulative Unique Users
The total number of distinct users who have signed in to CanadaLogin over a chosen reporting window: this month or this calendar year.
This metric is useful for understanding the overall reach and adoption of CanadaLogin over time. Note that it will not align with the sum of unique users across individual apps: a user who signs into App A and App B on the same day counts as two unique users at the app level but only one overall.
Alternative names:

month-to-date unique users
year-to-date unique users
total overall unique users this month / this year
overall unique users MTD / YTD
distinct people reached on CanadaLogin

Calculation. Take the latest value of the cumulative unique-user column for the window of interest. The window is chosen by which column you read, not by a date filter (see the note on reporting timespans):

mtd_unique_users for month-to-date
ytd_unique_users for year-to-date

These columns are cumulative, so the most recent row holds the current total.
A since_apr22_unique_users column (cumulative distinct users since launch) was previously available but has been removed; see the data retention note.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Month-to-date:
SELECT
    mtd_unique_users
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
ORDER BY from_date DESC
LIMIT 1;
Year-to-date:
SELECT
    ytd_unique_users
FROM ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
ORDER BY from_date DESC
LIMIT 1;


Month-to-date:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(mtd_unique_users)
Year-to-date:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify", "auth_total_logins")) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
